chapters.title: Introduction
chapters.html:
The starting price is the decision that most influences the outcome of your sale. Neither the price paid long ago, nor your renovations, nor your financial needs set the value: the market decides. The tool for reading it is called the comparative market analysis (CMA).

This guide explains how a CMA is built, why the municipal assessment isn't the value, and how the starting price influences the final price.

Each chapter ends with a lined « My notes » page to help you prepare YOUR pricing strategy.

chapters.title: What (really) determines value
chapters.objective: Distinguish market value from false reference points.
chapters.html:
Distinguish market value from false reference points.

Market value is the price an informed buyer is willing to pay today, under current market conditions. It has nothing to do with:

  • What you paid when you bought (the past doesn't interest the buyer).
  • The cost of your renovations (not all of them are recovered equally).
  • Your financial needs (the buyer doesn't care).
  • The municipal assessment (a tax tool, not a sale price).
Emilie's tip

Detach yourself from the « emotional » price. The market doesn't pay for your memories or your efforts, it pays what the property is worth today. It's sometimes hard to hear, but it's what gets a home sold.

chapters.title: The comparative market analysis (CMA)
chapters.objective: Understand how a fact-based price is built.
chapters.html:
Understand how a fact-based price is built.

The CMA compares your property to recent sales of similar properties in the same area: type, size, number of rooms, condition, garage, lot, etc. Adjustments are then made for the differences (a comparable property with an extra garage is worth a bit more, for example).

  • RECENT sales (the market moves) that are TRULY comparable.
  • Adjustments for objective differences.
  • You also look at properties currently for sale (your competition) and those that didn't find a buyer (often overpriced).
Emilie's tip

Be wary of « for sale » properties as a reference: anyone can ASK a price. It's SOLD properties that tell the true value.

chapters.title: Municipal assessment vs market value
chapters.objective: Don't confuse the tax tool with the sale price.
chapters.html:
Don't confuse the tax tool with the sale price.

The municipal assessment is used to calculate your taxes; it's established en masse, at a reference date, and can be higher or lower than the actual market value. The municipality even applies a « comparative factor » to try to bring it closer to the market.

Conclusion: never set your sale price based on the municipal assessment. It can serve as a clue, never as a verdict.

Emilie's tip

« My house is assessed at such-and-such by the city » is not a pricing argument. The municipal assessment and market value are two different things; only the market sets the sale price.

chapters.title: The starting-price strategy
chapters.objective: Choose a price that maximizes the final result.
chapters.html:
Choose a price that maximizes the final result.

A fair price, aligned with the CMA, quickly attracts buyers and can generate competition — which often drives the final price up. A price that's too high scares buyers off, the property stalls, and you end up lowering it… selling for less and later than with a good price from the start.

  • Good price from day 1: buzz, showings, offers, sometimes a bidding war.
  • Price too high: few showings, the image of a « property that lingers », successive drops.
  • The first serious buyer is often the best: don't let them slip away out of excessive optimism.
Emilie's tip

The market judges your price in the first two weeks. If showings are rare or bring no offer, it's almost always a matter of price — heed that signal early rather than late.

chapters.title: Action plan
chapters.html:
Your next steps, concretely.

This week

  1. Ask Emilie for a complete comparative analysis.
  2. List my renovations and check which ones add value.

Within 30 days

  1. Set a starting price aligned with recent sales.
  2. Define an adjustment plan in case the market doesn't respond.

Next

  1. Watch the signals (showings, offers) and react early.

chapters.title: Resources & glossary
chapters.html:
• Market value: the price an informed buyer pays under current conditions.
  • CMA: comparative market analysis, based on recent similar sales.
  • Adjustment: a price correction for differences between properties.
  • Municipal assessment: a tax value, different from the sale price.
  • Starting price: a strategic decision that influences the final price.
